posts.topic: Local spotlight: frost depth and footings in Larimer County
posts.caption:
30 inches. That's the minimum frost depth Larimer County's building department requires below grade, countywide.

Why it matters: water in the soil freezes and expands. A footing that bears above the frost line can lift every winter and settle every spring. That movement shows up as cracked slabs, sticking doors, and wall cracks that keep coming back.

Getting it right is cheap during excavation and expensive any time after.

What we check before the first footing is poured:
Bearing depth below frost, verified in the hole, not just on the drawings.
The soils report recommendations for the site.
Frost protection for footings and slabs when we pour in cold weather.
Inspection called and passed before the concrete shows up.

Each jurisdiction sets its own number, so confirm it with your building department before design.

Owners: on your last project, did anyone walk you through the foundation before it was buried?

posts.topic: Planning checklist: what to line up before design starts
posts.caption:
The most expensive surprises on a build show up before design ever starts. Here's the short list we want in hand before we draw anything:

Budget range that includes site work, utility fees, and permit costs, not just the building.
Boundary survey, so setbacks and easements are real.
Zoning and use check: allowed use, height, setbacks, parking, and design standards.
Utility availability and connection costs.
Geotechnical report, because foundation design starts with the soil.
Access: can a concrete truck and a crane get where they need to be?

None of this is glamorous. All of it changes what the building can be and what it costs.

posts.topic: Question of the week: what would you do differently on your last build?

Question of the week for owners, developers, and property managers:

We ask owners this at the start of a job. The answers usually aren't about finishes. They sound like:
Not enough power or data where the business actually needed it.
A loading or parking layout that never quite worked.
Storage and mechanical rooms sized too small.
Picking the low bid and paying for it later.

Your answer is the best design input there is. Drop it in the comments. If you're planning the next one, we're glad to talk it through before anything gets drawn.

posts.topic: Field tip: get the soils report before designing the foundation
posts.caption:
Field tip from the superintendent's side: never design a foundation before the soils report is in.

According to Colorado's Planning for Hazards program, about 50 percent of the state's soil has a high or very high potential to shrink and swell. Swelling clay can expand 10 percent or more as it gets wet, and that force goes straight into slabs and foundations.

The fix is simple compared to the damage:
Drill the site and get a geotechnical report.
Design the foundation and slab to the engineer's recommendations, whether that's overexcavation, a structural floor, or a different foundation type.
Grade the site so water runs away from the building, and keep it that way.

Testing is a small line item. Foundation repairs are not.

Owners: did your last project have a soils report before design, or after?
photo_brief: Excavation on site ("A teal excavator dumping soil into a yellow dump truck at a construction site")

posts.topic: Behind the build: how design-build keeps a budget honest
posts.caption:
The fastest way to kill a project: finish the design, send it out to bid, and find out it's over budget.

Here's how budgeting works on our design-build projects:

1. Set the budget first, including site, fees, and contingency.
2. Price the concept, not just finished drawings. Structural system, envelope, and MEP choices get costed early, when changes are cheap.
3. Update the estimate at each design milestone, so drift shows up in weeks, not after bids.
4. Make tradeoffs with the owner in the room: scope, quality, or schedule.

One team owns both the drawings and the number. Nobody gets to blame the other side.

Owners and developers: at what point on your last project did you find out what it was really going to cost?

posts.topic: This or that: slab-on-grade vs crawlspace
posts.caption:
Slab-on-grade or crawlspace? On a lot of Front Range projects, that's one of the first real design forks.

Slab-on-grade: fewer steps, lower profile, no void under the floor to ventilate or maintain. Utilities under the slab are hard to reach later.

Crawlspace with a structural floor: utilities stay accessible, and the floor is supported by the foundation instead of sitting on the soil. More steps, more cost, and a space that has to be detailed right.

On expansive soils, the geotechnical engineer's recommendation often makes this call for you. That's why we want the soils report before the foundation concept is set.

Which way did you go on your last build, and would you do it again?

posts.topic: Local spotlight: snow load climbs with elevation
posts.caption:
55 vs 160.

Those are Larimer County's design ground snow loads, in pounds per square foot, at 5,000 feet and at 9,000 feet. The county's table steps up with elevation: 70 at 6,000, 95 at 7,000, 110 at 8,000.

What that means for an owner:
Roof framing, trusses, and connections get heavier as you go up.
Pre-engineered and steel building packages have to be ordered to the number for the actual site, not a generic one. Drifting at roof steps and parapets adds load on top of that.

Same building, same county, different structure. And every mountain jurisdiction, from Winter Park to Steamboat to Vail, sets its own requirements.

We build on the Front Range and in the mountain towns. Owners planning a high-country project: has anyone talked to you yet about snow load on your site?

posts.topic: Planning checklist: getting a permit set ready
posts.caption:
A permit set that goes in incomplete comes back with comments, and every round of comments costs time. A checklist for owners getting ready to submit:

Zoning and use confirmed, with any planning or design review approvals in hand first.
Complete, stamped architectural and structural drawings.
Site plan with setbacks, drainage, utilities, and access.
Energy code compliance documentation.
Soils report, where the jurisdiction or engineer requires it.
Utility and fire department reviews where they apply.

Every jurisdiction has its own list, and the Front Range and the mountain towns don't run the same playbook. We pull the requirements before drawings are finished, so the set gets built to pass review.

posts.topic: Field tip: the cheapest change is the one made on paper
posts.caption:
Field tip: the cheapest change is the one made on paper.

A lot of change orders trace back to decisions that weren't made in time. From the field, the pattern is predictable:
Selections not finalized, so the trade waits or guesses.
Owner equipment and IT needs not defined, so power and data get moved after rough-in.
Scope assumptions not written down, so two people remember the deal differently.

What we do about it: a selections schedule tied to the construction schedule, written scope at every phase, and a decision log the owner can see.

It's not complicated. It just has to be done before the framers are standing there.

Estimating and value review while the design can still change.
Constructability review: catching conflicts between architectural, structural, and MEP drawings on paper instead of in the field.
Buyout: getting the right subcontractors committed.
Long-lead procurement, so equipment and materials don't become the critical path.
A schedule built with the people who'll actually do the work.

posts.topic: This or that: metal building vs wood frame for a shop or warehouse
posts.caption:
Metal building or wood frame for your next shop or warehouse?

Pre-engineered metal: big clear spans, fast erection once the package lands, noncombustible. The package has to be engineered for the exact site, and lead time on the steel can drive the schedule.

Wood frame or post-frame: familiar to local crews, easy to modify, often a lower first cost at smaller sizes. Span, height, and use can push it past what makes sense.

The right answer depends on clear height, span, what's going inside, and what code and your insurer will allow.

Keep site access clear so deliveries and inspectors can actually get in.

posts.topic: This or that: open office vs private offices in a tenant finish
posts.caption:
Tenant finish question: open office or private offices?

Open plan: fewer walls, more flexibility, usually less drywall, doors, and ductwork to run. Noise and privacy become the problems to solve.

Private offices: quiet and confidential, easier for client meetings. More walls, more doors, more HVAC zones, more cost, and harder to rearrange later.

Most spaces end up as a mix. The trick is deciding where the walls go before the ductwork, lighting, and power get laid out around them.

Staging space is tight, so deliveries have to be timed, not dumped.
Access roads and weather decide when trucks can get up.
Crews may travel, so lodging and drive time hit the schedule.
The building season is shorter, so the plan has to be tighter.
Every jurisdiction and many communities have their own review requirements.

None of that is a reason not to build. It's a reason to plan it like a superintendent would.

posts.topic: This or that: lump sum vs cost-plus with a GMP
posts.caption:
Two common ways to price a construction contract. Which do you prefer?

Lump sum: one fixed price for a defined scope. Clear number up front. Works best when the design is complete. Changes get priced one at a time.

Cost-plus with a guaranteed maximum price (GMP): you pay actual cost plus a fee, up to a cap. Open books. Works well when you want to start before every detail is drawn.

Neither is better every time. The right fit depends on how complete the design is, how much risk you want to carry, and how much visibility you want into the numbers.

posts.topic: Local spotlight: know which building department you're in
posts.caption:

A property just outside city limits can fall under the county instead of the city, and the two can have different code amendments, submittal requirements, review times, and inspection processes. Loveland, Fort Collins, Windsor, Berthoud, Larimer County, and Weld County each run their own show.

Before design starts, we confirm:
Which jurisdiction the parcel is in.
Which code editions and local amendments apply.
What the zoning allows.
What the submittal checklist looks like.

It sounds basic. It saves weeks.

posts.topic: Field tip: protect water lines during winter construction
posts.caption:
Field tip: a building under construction can freeze just like a finished one, and it's usually less protected.

Once water lines are charged, a cold snap can split a pipe inside a wall before anyone notices. The damage shows up later as wet drywall, ruined insulation, and rework.

What we watch:
Keep temporary heat running in enclosed areas once lines are charged.
Don't charge lines before the space can be kept above freezing.
Drain and protect lines in areas that can't be heated.
Check the building after every cold night, not just on Monday.

Owners: has freeze damage ever hit one of your projects?

posts.topic: Behind the build: what single point of responsibility means
posts.caption:
"Single point of responsibility" gets thrown around in design-build. Here's what it actually means when something goes wrong.

In a traditional setup, a problem in the field starts a debate. The contractor says the drawings were wrong. The designer says the contractor built it wrong. The owner sits in the middle, paying for the time it takes to figure out who's responsible.

In design-build, the design and the construction come from the same team under one contract. If there's a conflict, it's ours to solve. No finger-pointing, no change order for someone else's mistake.

posts.topic: This or that: polished concrete vs LVT flooring in commercial space
posts.caption:
Commercial flooring: polished concrete or luxury vinyl tile (LVT)?

Polished concrete: tough, low maintenance, and the slab is already there. Needs to be planned before the pour, and it shows every crack and patch.

LVT: warmer and quieter underfoot, lots of looks, easy to replace a damaged piece. Needs a flat, dry slab, and moisture in the concrete can cause problems if it isn't tested.

For shops and warehouses, concrete usually wins. For offices and retail, it's a closer call.

posts.topic: Local spotlight: Northern Colorado wind on the jobsite
posts.caption:
Anyone who has built in Northern Colorado knows: the wind is part of the schedule.

On a windy site we plan for:
Temporary bracing on framed walls until the structure ties together.
Securing sheathing, insulation, and anything else that can turn into a sail.
Crane and lift days that may get called off.
Roofing and wrap that can't go on in high wind.
Dust control for the neighbors.

A wind day isn't a lost day if the crew has inside work lined up. That's the superintendent's job: always have a plan B on the board.

posts.topic: Field tip: the three-week lookahead
posts.caption:

Which trades need to be on site.

The job isn't done when the last wall gets painted. It's done when the owner has everything they need to run the building.

A good closeout includes:

Final inspections and certificate of occupancy.
Warranties from every trade and manufacturer.
Operation and maintenance manuals for equipment.

Attic stock of finishes for future repairs.

posts.topic: Field tip: manage water on the site during construction
posts.caption:
Field tip: the drainage plan doesn't start when the landscaping goes in. It starts the day the dirt gets moved.

During construction we watch:
Keep water from ponding against open foundations.
Grade away from the building early, even if it's temporary.
Protect excavations from runoff during storms and snowmelt.
Keep downspouts discharging away from the building as soon as the roof is on.
Keep stormwater controls in place so mud doesn't leave the site.

Water sitting against a foundation during construction can cause problems that don't show up until years later.

posts.topic: Behind the build: allowances explained
posts.caption:
An allowance is a placeholder number in a construction contract for something that hasn't been picked yet. Flooring, light fixtures, cabinets, hardware.

Allowances are useful. They let the project move forward before every selection is made. They're also one of the biggest sources of budget surprises.

How we handle them:
Set allowances based on what the owner actually wants, not the cheapest option.
Spell out what each allowance includes: material only, or material and labor.
Review selections against the allowance before they're ordered, not after.

posts.topic: This or that: radiant floor heat vs forced air in a shop
posts.caption:
Heating a shop: radiant floor or forced air?

Radiant floor: warm slab, even heat, nothing blowing dust around. Recovers well when big doors open and close. Has to be decided before the slab is poured, and it costs more up front.

Forced air or unit heaters: lower first cost, heats up fast, can be added or changed later. Warm air rises, so the floor where you're working can stay cold.

The decision usually comes down to door size, how the space is used, and budget.

Which would you put in your shop, and why?

posts.caption:
Expanding a commercial or industrial building? Check your utilities before you design.

Electrical: what's your current service size, and how much is left? New equipment can mean a service upgrade, and that can have a long lead time.
Gas: will the meter and line handle new heaters or process equipment?
Water and sewer: will new fixtures or processes push you over what you have?
Fire: does the addition trigger a sprinkler or alarm requirement?
Data: where does it come in, and where does it need to go?

Utility upgrades are often the longest-lead item on an expansion.

Owners: has a utility upgrade ever held up one of your projects?

posts.topic: Question of the week: the best-built building you've been in
posts.caption:
Question of the week:

What's the best-built building you've ever been in, and what made it great?

Maybe it was quiet. Maybe the light was right. Maybe everything just worked, and you could tell someone cared about the details.

We ask because the answers are a great design brief. The things people remember are rarely the expensive finishes. They're layout, light, comfort, and how well the building fits the people in it.

Tell us yours in the comments.

posts.topic: Field tip: mockups and samples for finishes
posts.caption:
Field tip: never approve a finish from a picture.

Before a finish goes on the whole building, we want a sample or a mockup in the actual space:
A section of paint on the real wall, in the real light.
A sample panel of siding or masonry.
A tile layout dry-fit before it's set.
A sample of the concrete finish.

Colors change under different light. Textures look different at full scale. A small mockup costs very little compared to redoing a whole wall.

Owners: have you ever approved a finish that looked different once it was installed?

posts.topic: Behind the build: value engineering done right
posts.caption:
Value engineering has a bad reputation, because it often just means cutting quality to hit a number.

Done right, it means getting the same function for less money. Examples:
A different structural system that does the same job with less material.
A simpler roof shape that drains just as well.
Standard sizes that cut waste.
A mechanical system sized to the actual load, not a rule of thumb.

The key is timing. In design-build, we look for these during design, when changes cost a few hours of drawing time instead of torn-out work.

Owners: has value engineering ever cost you something you wish you'd kept?

posts.topic: This or that: standing seam metal roof vs asphalt shingles
posts.caption:
Roofing question: standing seam metal or asphalt shingles?

Standing seam metal: long life, sheds snow, few exposed fasteners. Higher first cost, and snow sliding off needs to be planned for over doors and walkways.

Asphalt shingles: lower first cost, familiar, easy to repair. Shorter life, and wind and hail can do damage.

In Colorado, hail, wind, and snow all factor in, and your insurer may have an opinion too.

Which would you pick, and why?

posts.topic: Local spotlight: short December days on the jobsite
posts.caption:
December daylight on the Front Range is short, and it changes how a job runs.

What we adjust:
Start times move with the light and the temperature.
Temporary lighting goes up inside and at access points.
Exterior work that needs daylight gets scheduled into the middle of the day.
Crews wear high-visibility gear for the dark mornings and evenings.
Inspections get scheduled early, before the day runs out.

Short days don't have to mean lost days. They mean the schedule has to be smarter.

Builders: how do you adjust your crew's day in winter?

posts.topic: Planning checklist: write your program before the first design meeting
posts.caption:
Before your first design meeting, write down your program. It's the most useful thing an owner can bring.

A good program answers:
Who uses the building, and how many people?
What rooms or spaces do you need, and roughly how big?
What equipment goes in, and what does it need: power, air, water, door size?
How do people, products, and vehicles move through the building?
What do you expect to need in five to ten years?

It doesn't have to be fancy. A spreadsheet or a page of notes works. It gives the design a real starting point.

posts.topic: Field tip: submittals matter
posts.caption:
Field tip: submittals are boring, and they matter.

A submittal is the contractor's proof of exactly which product, model, or material is going in, sent to the designer for review before it's ordered. Doors, hardware, HVAC units, roofing, windows, light fixtures.

Why it matters:
It catches the wrong product before it shows up on site.
It confirms sizes, ratings, and colors.
It flags long lead times early.
It creates a record of what was approved.

A missing submittal is how the wrong door ends up in the wrong opening.

Owners: do you see the submittals on your projects?

posts.topic: This or that: build new or renovate existing?
posts.caption:
Build new or renovate what you have?

Renovate: often faster to occupy, keeps your location, may cost less for the shell. But existing buildings hide surprises, and code upgrades can be triggered by the work.

Build new: designed around exactly how you work, new systems, better efficiency. Needs land, a longer timeline, and full site work.

The answer usually comes down to the condition of the existing building, how well it fits your operation, and your timeline.

Owners: if you had to choose today, which way would you go?

posts.topic: Local spotlight: winter is planning season
posts.caption:
In Northern Colorado and the mountain towns, winter is when the best spring projects get made.

While the ground is frozen, owners can:

Get the soils report and survey done when the ground allows.
Submit for permits and work through review comments.
Lock in subcontractors and order long-lead materials.

When the weather turns, those projects are ready to go. Projects that start planning in spring often find themselves breaking ground much later.

posts.topic: Field tip: how to do a good punch list
posts.caption:
Field tip: a punch list is the list of small items to fix before a job is done. A good one finishes the job. A bad one drags on for months.

How to do it right:
Walk room by room, top to bottom, in good light.
Be specific: location, issue, who fixes it.
Take a photo of each item.
Assign a date to each item.
Re-walk and sign off each item as it's done.

Best of all: keep the list short by running quality checks during construction, not just at the end.

Owners: how long did your last punch list take to close?

posts.topic: Behind the build: from sketch to keys, the phases
posts.caption:
From napkin sketch to keys in hand, here's how a design-build project moves:

2. Concept design: layout and massing, with a budget check.
3. Design development: systems and materials chosen, priced again.
4. Construction documents: the full set for permit and construction.
5. Permitting: submittal, comments, approval.
6. Construction: site work through finishes.
7. Closeout: inspections, punch list, warranties, training.

Same team the whole way. The people who priced it are the people who build it.

posts.topic: Planning checklist: building a real budget
posts.caption:
A real construction budget has more than one number. Here's what it should include:

Hard costs: the building itself and the site work.
Soft costs: design, engineering, surveys, soils report, permits, fees, and inspections.
Utility costs: connection fees and service upgrades.
Furniture, fixtures, and equipment, if you're providing them.
Financing costs, if you're borrowing.
Contingency: money set aside for the unknown, because there's always something.

Budgets that only count the building are the ones that get blown.

posts.topic: Field tip: be ready for inspections
posts.caption:
Field tip: a failed inspection costs more than the reinspection fee. It costs days.

How we get inspections passed the first time:
Walk the work ourselves before calling the inspection.
Have the approved plans and any engineering on site.
Make the work accessible: ladders, lighting, clear paths.
Don't call it early hoping it'll pass.
Fix comments the same day when possible.

Inspectors are part of the team. Treat their time with respect and the whole job moves faster.

Conflicts between drawings found in the field.

posts.topic: This or that: build it in phases or all at once?
posts.caption:
Last this or that of the year: build in phases or all at once?

Phased: spreads out the cost, lets you build what you need now and add later. Each phase has its own mobilization, and the future phase needs to be planned now so it connects cleanly.

All at once: one mobilization, often a lower total cost, done sooner. Bigger cash need up front.

The key is designing the full build-out at the start, even if you only build part of it.

Owners: are you more of a phase it or build it all now type?

posts.topic: Field tip: order long-lead items early
posts.caption:

posts.topic: This or that: one story or two?
posts.caption:
One story or two?

One story: no stairs or elevator, simpler structure, easier to expand later, easier access for everyone. Needs more land and more roof and foundation per square foot.

Two story: smaller footprint, more space on less land, less roof and foundation. Adds stairs, possibly an elevator for commercial use, and more structure.

The site, the use, and the budget usually make the call.

Which would you choose for your next building?

posts.topic: Local spotlight: snow and site access on winter builds
posts.caption:
In January, the most important thing on a Colorado jobsite can be a clear road in.

What we plan for on winter sites:
Snow removal: who plows, and how fast after a storm.
Where the snow goes, so it doesn't bury materials or melt into the excavation.
Safe walking paths and stair access, salted and cleared.
Truck access for concrete, deliveries, and dumpsters.
Getting inspectors in and out.

A site that can't be reached can't be built.

Builders: what's your snow plan on a winter job?

posts.topic: Field tip: walk the site before design starts
posts.caption:
Field tip: walk the site with your builder before the design starts.

What a superintendent looks for:
Where trucks and equipment get in.
Where materials can be staged.
Overhead lines and buried utilities.
Grade and drainage: where water goes.
Neighbors, noise, and dust concerns.
Trees, rock, or anything that will make excavation harder.
